name: Joint Service Commendation Medal
deviceExplanation: Two awards. Joint medals use an oak-leaf cluster, not a star. One bronze oak leaf means the second award.
explanation: A mid-level decoration from a joint command, one that includes more than one branch of the military. It sits above the service achievement medals and beside the Navy Commendation Medal.
criteria: Meritorious achievement or service while assigned to a joint activity. It is not a valor award unless a V device is authorized. There is no V on this ribbon.
sourceNote: Joint Service Commendation Medal (2). One in 2013, and one in December 2014.

name: Navy and Marine Corps Commendation Medal
deviceExplanation: One award, so the ribbon is worn with no star.
explanation: The Navy and Marine Corps version of a commendation medal. It recognizes meritorious service or a specific achievement. On a rack it is worn just after the Joint Service Commendation Medal. Army commendations of the same level come after it.
criteria: Meritorious service or achievement. No V device.
sourceNote: One Navy and Marine Corps Commendation Medal (NC), no V. Worksheet year: 2018.

name: Army Commendation Medal
deviceExplanation: Two awards. The Army uses a bronze oak-leaf cluster for the second award, not a gold star.
explanation: The Army's commendation medal. Sailors receive it when they are serving with the Army, which happened on the individual-augmentee tour and in joint commands. Navy rules place an Army award of this level immediately after the Navy commendation medal.
criteria: Meritorious service or achievement recognized by the Army.
sourceNote: Army Commendation Medal (2). Worksheet years: 2009 and 2011.

name: Joint Service Achievement Medal
deviceExplanation: One award. No device.
explanation: A joint-service decoration below the commendation medals. It recognizes meritorious achievement or service of a lesser scope than a commendation medal, still in a multi-service command.
criteria: Meritorious achievement or service in a joint assignment.
sourceNote: One Joint Service Achievement Medal. Worksheet year: 2013.

name: Navy and Marine Corps Achievement Medal
deviceExplanation: Five awards. The ribbon itself is the first. Each award after that is a gold star, so four gold stars means five awards. A fifth gold star would have been replaced by one silver star.
explanation: The Navy and Marine Corps achievement medal. For a sailor, this is the common personal decoration for a strong tour or a particular piece of work. Five of them is a long record of that kind of recognition.
criteria: Meritorious service or achievement of a degree below a commendation medal.

name: Army Achievement Medal
deviceExplanation: One award. No oak leaf.
explanation: The Army's achievement medal, junior to the Army Commendation Medal. It is worn after the Navy achievement medal because Navy rules put the other service's equivalent just behind the Navy award.
criteria: Meritorious service or achievement recognized by the Army.
sourceNote: Army Achievement Medal, one award. Worksheet year: 2006.

name: Joint Meritorious Unit Award
deviceExplanation: Three awards. The gold frame is part of the award. Two bronze oak-leaf clusters mark the second and third awards.
explanation: A unit award, not a personal medal. Everyone assigned to the cited joint unit for the right dates may wear it. The ribbon is worn inside a gold frame. It comes before Navy unit awards on a Navy rack.
criteria: The unit, not the individual, is cited for exceptionally meritorious achievement. You wear it if you were assigned there during the cited period.
sourceNote: Joint Meritorious Unit Award (3), all while assigned to JCSE. Headquarters, U.S. Joint Forces Command, 1 February 2008–6 August 2010, JCSE named (Army GO 2013-11, https://armypubs.army.mil/epubs/DR_pubs/DR_a/pdf/web/go1311.pdf); Headquarters, CJSOTF-A, 1 April 2010–15 May 2011, OEF 2010–11 (Army GO 2013-11, https://armypubs.army.mil/epubs/DR_pubs/DR_a/pdf/web/go1311.pdf); Headquarters, SOJTF-A, 26 July 2012–14 June 2013, OEF 2012–13 (Army GO 2016-02, https://armypubs.army.mil/epubs/DR_pubs/DR_a/pdf/web/go1602.pdf).

name: Navy Meritorious Unit Commendation
deviceExplanation: Five awards. Navy unit awards use bronze stars, not oak leaves. Four bronze stars mean five awards. A silver star would appear only on a sixth award.
explanation: A Navy unit award for meritorious service by a ship or command. It is junior to the Navy Unit Commendation, which is not in this record, and senior to the Navy E ribbon.
criteria: Worn by members of a cited Navy unit for the period of the citation.
sourceNote: Navy Meritorious Unit Commendation (5). DD-214 count is official. Allocation (Oct 18 2026; Sergio reported aboard USS Frank Cable before July 2001): USS Frank Cable 4, unit citation periods July 1999–July 2001, August 2001–July 2003, July 2002–January 2003 and August 2003–July 2005 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Frank_Cable_(AS-40); https://www.navsource.org/archives/09/36/3640.htm); EODMU 5 1 (no public citation found). The worksheet named 2000, inside the first Frank Cable period.

name: Navy E Ribbon
deviceExplanation: Three awards, each a 3/16 in silver Battle E: a plain block letter, smaller than the marksmanship E. A fourth award would replace the three letters with one wreathed E. That is not the case here.
explanation: The Battle Effectiveness ribbon. A ship or unit wins it by placing at the top of its group in an annual competition of readiness and skill. The people assigned there when it is won may wear the ribbon.
criteria: Permanent duty in a unit that won the battle-efficiency competition.
sourceNote: Navy E Ribbon (3). Worksheet years: 2001, 2002, and 2003, the Frank Cable years. Confirmed by Sergio through the Admin LPO of the time (Oct 17 2026): all three Battle E awards are from USS Frank Cable (AS-40), 2001, 2002 and 2003. This supersedes the Wikipedia listing, which shows only 2001 and 2002 in this period.

name: Navy Good Conduct Medal
deviceExplanation: Six awards. In Navy rules a silver star replaces five gold stars. The ribbon is the first award and the silver star stands for the next five, which is six altogether.
explanation: Given for a period of honorable active service with good performance marks and no serious disciplinary action. For most of this career each medal covered three years. Six medals line up with a twenty-year career.
criteria: A qualifying period of good conduct. The worksheet lists 2000, 2003, 2006, 2009, 2012, and 2015.
sourceNote: Navy Good Conduct Medal (6).

name: National Defense Service Medal
deviceExplanation: One award. No star. A second award, for an earlier war period, would be a bronze star. Service here falls in the period that began in 2001.
explanation: Given to people serving on active duty during a designated time of war or national emergency. It does not by itself mean the person deployed. For this career it marks service after the 11 September 2001 attacks.
criteria: Active duty during a qualifying period. The worksheet dates it 2001 and labels it Global War on Terror.
sourceNote: National Defense Service Medal, one award.

name: Afghanistan Campaign Medal
deviceExplanation: One medal. Each campaign phase wears a bronze star. There is no bare ribbon. Two OEF phases, two stars. These are not gold stars as on a Navy achievement medal.
explanation: For service in Afghanistan during named operations, here Operation Enduring Freedom. Two bronze stars for the two Afghanistan tours, 2010–2011 and 2012–2013.
criteria: Service in the theater during a qualifying campaign phase. Each phase is a star.
sourceNote: Afghanistan Campaign Medal with two campaign stars. The worksheet lists the medal once, in 2011, and two OEF tours.

name: Iraq Campaign Medal
deviceExplanation: One medal. Each campaign phase wears a bronze star. There is no bare ribbon. National Resolution (2006) is one star; Iraq Sovereignty (the IA, in country 2009) is the second.
explanation: For service in Iraq during Operation Iraqi Freedom. Two bronze stars for the two Iraq phases: Combined Joint Task Force Troy in 2006, and the individual augmentee tour that started in October 2008 (five months at Fort Bliss, then Joint Base Balad).
criteria: Service in Iraq during a qualifying campaign phase. Each phase is a star.
sourceNote: Iraq Campaign Medal with two campaign stars. The worksheet lists the medal in 2006 and names both phases under operations.

name: Global War on Terrorism Service Medal
deviceExplanation: One award.
explanation: For support of operations against terrorism on or after 11 September 2001, including duty that was not inside Iraq or Afghanistan. It is different from the campaign medals, which require service in those countries, and from the expeditionary medal, which is not in this record.
criteria: Qualifying support service. The worksheet dates it 2005.
sourceNote: GWOT Service Medal, one award.

name: Humanitarian Service Medal
deviceExplanation: One award. No star.
explanation: For taking part in a military operation whose purpose was humanitarian. The storm was Typhoon Pongsona, Guam, December 2002. The worksheet dated the medal 2003; the award is December 2002.
criteria: Direct participation in a designated humanitarian operation. Storm: Typhoon Pongsona, December 2002. Worksheet year: 2003.
sourceNote: Humanitarian Service Medal, one award. Typhoon Pongsona.

name: Sea Service Deployment Ribbon
deviceExplanation: Seven awards. These ribbons use bronze stars, and a silver star replaces five bronze stars. Seven awards show as one silver star and one bronze star.
explanation: For deployed sea duty. In general it marks accumulated time deployed away from home port, often counted in months at sea or forward. Seven awards is a great deal of deployed time. Sea service of 6 years, 4 months, and 24 days is the total time, not the ribbon count.
criteria: Qualifying deployed sea service for each award.
sourceNote: Sea Service Deployment Ribbon (7). DD-214 count is official. The worksheet names 2001, 2002, and 2003; four years are not entered. Allocation (Oct 17 2026, inferred where the year is not on the worksheet): USS Frank Cable 3 (2001–2003, overseas-homeported ship), OIF 2006 1, IA tour 2008–09 1, JCSE OEF 2010–11 and 2012–13 2. Criteria: SECNAVINST 1650.1 (SSDR).

name: Navy and Marine Corps Overseas Service Ribbon
deviceExplanation: Six awards. One silver star stands in for five bronze stars, so the ribbon plus the silver star is six awards.
explanation: For a completed tour at an overseas shore station, generally twelve months. It is not the same as the sea-service ribbon, which is for deployments. Guam is the overseas shore duty in this record; the form does not say which tours made up all six awards.
criteria: A qualifying overseas shore tour for each award.
sourceNote: Navy and Marine Corps Overseas Ribbon (6). DD-214 count is official. The worksheet names 2001, 2002, and 2003; three years are not entered. Allocation (Oct 17 2026, inferred where the year is not on the worksheet): USS Frank Cable 3 (2001–2003), EODMU 5 3 (Guam, 2004–2007). Criteria: SECNAVINST 1650.1 (OSR: 12 months overseas duty; Navy overseas-homeported units may hold both SSDR and OSR after 1 Oct 1999).

name: NATO Medal (ISAF)
deviceExplanation: One NATO medal. The ribbon shown is the Non-Article 5 ribbon used for ISAF. The ISAF clasp is noted in the record; it is not drawn as a separate device here.
explanation: A foreign award, from NATO rather than the United States, for service with the International Security Assistance Force in Afghanistan. Foreign awards are worn after U.S. service awards and before the marksmanship awards.
criteria: Service with ISAF under the rules NATO set for the medal. Worksheet: 2013, Non-Article 5, Afghanistan.
sourceNote: NATO Medal, one award.

name: Navy Expert Rifleman Medal
deviceExplanation: Expert is the top of three levels: Marksman, Sharpshooter, Expert. The ribbon carries the 1/4 in silver Expert E, a heavy slab-serif letter that differs from the Battle E.
explanation: The Navy's medal for Expert qualification with the service rifle on the Navy qualification course, the highest of the three levels. Its ribbon carries the Expert E and is worn at the very end of the rack, after every decoration and every foreign award.
criteria: Expert qualification on the rifle course. Worksheet year: 2001.
sourceNote: Navy Expert Rifleman Medal.

name: Navy Expert Pistol Shot Medal
deviceExplanation: Expert with the service pistol, shown with the 1/4 in silver Expert E (slab-serif, larger than the Battle E).
explanation: The pistol counterpart of the Expert Rifleman Medal: Expert qualification with the service pistol, the highest of the three levels. Its ribbon carries the Expert E and is worn after the rifle award.
criteria: Expert qualification on the pistol course. Worksheet year: 2000.
sourceNote: Navy Expert Pistol Shot Medal.
